prompt: Which questions does “Great write-up, Paula!” leave unanswered? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Great in what way?
choices.why: Yes: speed, tone, accuracy or length?

choices.text: Who wrote it?
choices.why: No: the message names Paula.

choices.text: Great compared with what?
choices.why: Yes: better than usual, or the expected bar?

choices.text: Great for whom?
choices.why: Yes: did it matter to anybody?

choices.text: Was Renata sincere?
choices.why: No: the lesson grants it was sincere; the problem is the information.

prompt: What does the lesson mean by calling positive feedback calibration?
hint: People learn what a team values from what it notices.

choices.text: It balances the negative feedback given in the same week, so the person’s mood stays level
choices.why: That is the ratio idea the next section takes apart.

choices.text: It adjusts the person’s pay
choices.why: Pay is not mentioned.

choices.text: What good looks like
choices.why: Right: corrective feedback teaches what to avoid; specific praise shows the top of the range.

choices.text: It measures how motivated the team is
choices.why: It is not a measurement of the team.

prompt: Two weeks after Renata praised Yara’s design document in public, Thiago’s first design document had a section on what he considered and dropped. What does that show?
hint: Nobody asked him to add it.

choices.text: Thiago copied Yara
choices.why: He adopted a practice, which is what calibration is for.

choices.text: Renata had told Thiago privately to add it to every design document he writes from now on
choices.why: The lesson says nobody asked him.

choices.text: Design documents at Caju have a template
choices.why: No template is mentioned; the change came from the praise.

choices.text: The precise praise told the whole team what a design document at Caju should contain, without anybody writing a rule
choices.why: Right: praising Yara precisely calibrated the whole team.

prompt: In Mueller and Dweck’s 1998 study, what happened to children praised for being clever?

choices.text: They worked harder
choices.why: The children praised for effort were the ones who kept taking on harder tasks.

choices.text: They chose easier tasks afterwards, and did worse after a failure
choices.why: Right: praise for a trait teaches people to protect the label.

choices.text: Nothing measurable
choices.why: The study found a clear difference.

choices.text: They asked for more praise
choices.why: Not what the study reported.

prompt: Which praise follows the lesson’s advice best?

choices.text: “You’re a natural at incident writing, and everybody on the team knows it.”
choices.why: Praise for a trait, which makes the next hard incident a risk to the label.

choices.text: “Great job as always!”
choices.why: Vague, and “as always” tells her nothing about this one.

choices.text: “Putting the cause last was the right call.”
choices.why: Right: it names a choice Paula can repeat on purpose.

choices.text: “You’re so good with clinics.”
choices.why: Another trait, with nothing to repeat.

prompt: What happened to the mathematical model behind the positivity ratio?

choices.text: It was confirmed by a larger study
choices.why: It was critiqued and the modelling withdrawn.

choices.text: It was refined to 5 to 1
choices.why: Numbers like that are folk versions; no refinement rescued the model.

choices.text: It was withdrawn
choices.why: Right: Brown, Sokal and Friedman showed the equations did not fit, and the journal withdrew the modelling.

choices.text: It was adopted by most management courses as the standard rule for how often to praise
choices.why: It spread before the critique; adoption is not what happened to the model.

prompt: Why does the feedback sandwich stop working after a few uses?
hint: What does the first compliment start to mean?

choices.text: The criticism gets lost in the middle
choices.why: That happens too, but the lesson’s first point is that people learn the pattern.

choices.text: People learn the pattern, and start hearing any compliment from that manager as the warning before a “but”
choices.why: Right: praise becomes the signal that a “but” is coming, so it no longer works on its own.

choices.text: Managers run out of compliments
choices.why: Not the problem described.

choices.text: It takes too long to prepare three parts for every piece of feedback you need to give
choices.why: Time is not the objection; the pattern and the lost message are.

prompt: Renata counts positive and corrective feedback per person each month. What is she looking for?

choices.text: Anybody who has heard only one kind
choices.why: Right: somebody who hears only corrections gets a false picture of what she thinks.

choices.text: Whether each person gets at least three positives per negative
choices.why: She is explicitly not aiming at a ratio.

choices.text: Who deserves a bonus
choices.why: Nothing about bonuses.

choices.text: Which people are performing worst on the team, so she can start improvement plans early
choices.why: The count is about the picture her feedback gives, not ranking performance.

prompt: The feedback ___ wraps criticism between two compliments.
What does public recognition do that private recognition does not?

choices.text: Counts more towards promotion
choices.why: Nothing says promotion weighs public praise more.

choices.text: Is always more welcome to the person
choices.why: Some people dislike it, which is the first risk the lesson names.

choices.text: Tells the team what is valued
choices.why: Right: it recognises the person and calibrates everybody else.

choices.text: Replaces the need for any specific detail, since the audience already knows what happened
choices.why: Public praise needs precision too, especially about who did what.

prompt: Match each way public praise backfires with its fix.

pairs.right: ask early how they prefer to hear it

pairs.left: it always goes to the same people

prompt: Why does the lesson say “that’s what I’d expect from a senior engineer” carries more than enthusiasm?
hint: A scale the person cares about.

choices.text: It promises a promotion
choices.why: It does not, and lesson 24 warns against promises like that.

choices.text: It is said in public, where the rest of the team can hear what the expected level is
choices.why: It can be said privately; its value is the scale, not the audience.

choices.text: It is longer
choices.why: Length is not the point.

choices.text: It places the work on a written scale
choices.why: Right: it says where the work sits against what is expected, which lesson 11 writes down.

prompt: At the demo, a manager says: “Huge thanks to Camila for the new booking screen!” Camila presented it; Fábio wrote most of the code and does not like attention. What went wrong?

choices.text: Nothing: thanking the presenter is enough
choices.why: The person who did the work sees it, and so does everybody who knows.

choices.text: The credit went to the presenter, not the author, and Fábio needed a private thank-you that said what he did
choices.why: Right: be precise about who did what, and use the channel the person prefers.

choices.text: She should have thanked the whole team instead
choices.why: “Thanks, team” avoids the wrong name and still credits nobody precisely.

choices.text: Praise should never be given at a demo
choices.why: Demos are a fine place for public recognition, done precisely.
